        <h1>Yŏm Sŭngik <span class="yom-hanja" lang="zh-Hant">廉承益</span></h1>
        <p class="yom-hero-lead">Power, devotion, and artistic production at the court of King Ch’ungnyŏl <span class="yom-hanja" lang="zh-Hant">忠烈王</span>.</p>
        <p class="yom-hero-note">A high official, interpreter of Mongolian, close associate of the ruler, and devout Buddhist, Yŏm Sŭngik (?–1302) provides an exceptional vantage point on the links between court, monasteries, stupa restoration, sūtra copying, and image commissioning in Koryŏ.</p>

  <section class="yom-section" id="portrait"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">01 · A man of the court</div><h2>Yŏm Sŭngik at the heart of Ch’ungnyŏl’s reign</h2>
      <p>Yŏm Sŭngik’s biography in the <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span> places him among the ruler’s close associates. His career reached a decisive turning point in 1277, when he accompanied King Ch’ungnyŏl to the monastery of Ch’ŏnhyo <span class="yom-hanja">天孝寺</span> during the king’s illness and took part in his care. Yet Yŏm Sŭngik’s role extended beyond the court: he also became an intermediary between royal power and Buddhist institutions.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="yom-intro-grid">
      <div><p>Yŏm Sŭngik spoke Mongolian and served as an interpreter for envoys arriving from Dadu. He thus belonged to the group of high officials who mediated between the kingdom of Koryŏ and the Yuan court. At the same time, his Buddhist devotion took material form through donations, ritual practices, and artistic commissions.</p>
      <p>This dual position explains his importance: Yŏm Sŭngik cannot be reduced either to a private commissioner or to his administrative role alone. He connected <strong>royal authority, administrative resources, monasteries, artisans, copyists, and votive practices</strong>.</p>
      <p class="yom-source">Principal source: <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a, biography of Yŏm Sŭngik in the section on “favorites”; Bryan Sauvadet’s dissertation, chap. 1, § 1.1.2.2.1.</p></div>
      <aside class="yom-profile-card" aria-label="Biographical landmarks"><div class="yom-profile-name">Yŏm Sŭngik</div><div class="yom-profile-hanja yom-hanja">廉承益</div>

          <div class="yom-profile-fact"><b>Roles</b><span>High official, interpreter, court intimate</span></div><div class="yom-profile-fact"><b>Devotion</b><span>Monasteries, sūtras, images, rites, and healing</span></div>

  <section class="yom-section" id="chronologie"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">02 · Interactive chronology</div><h2>A career between court, monasteries, and Buddhist commissions</h2><p>Filter the events to isolate the different dimensions of Yŏm Sŭngik’s trajectory.</p></div>
    <figure class="yom-map-insert yom-map-insert--compact">
      <img src="/assets/img/yom-sungik/map-parcours-1277-1283.webp" alt="Map of Yŏm Sŭngik’s religious and administrative movements in Kaegyŏng between 1277 and 1283." loading="lazy">
      <figcaption><strong>Yŏm Sŭngik’s religious and administrative routes, 1277–1283.</strong> The map brings together the principal movements that structure the first part of his career: Ch’ŏnhyo, Hyŏnhwa, the royal scriptorium, and the 1283 restoration circuit.</figcaption>
    </figure>
    <div class="yom-timeline-tools" role="group" aria-label="Chronology filters">
      <button class="yom-filter active" type="button" data-filter="all" aria-pressed="true">All</button>
      <button class="yom-filter" type="button" data-filter="cour" aria-pressed="false">Court</button>
      <button class="yom-filter" type="button" data-filter="monastere" aria-pressed="false">Monasteries</button>
      <button class="yom-filter" type="button" data-filter="commande" aria-pressed="false">Commissions</button>
      <button class="yom-filter" type="button" data-filter="rituel" aria-pressed="false">Ritual & healing</button>
    </div>
    <div class="yom-timeline">
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour rituel"><div class="yom-event-year">1277</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>At the side of the ailing king</h3><p>Yŏm Sŭngik accompanies Ch’ungnyŏl to the monastery of Ch’ŏnhyo <span class="yom-hanja">天孝寺</span> and takes part in the ruler’s care. The episode strengthens his proximity to the king.</p><p class="yom-source"><em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">court</span><span class="yom-tag">healing</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour"><div class="yom-event-year">1278</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Political ascent</h3><p>Royal favor brings promotion and admission into circles where affairs of the kingdom are deliberated.</p><p class="yom-source"><em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">court</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour monastere"><div class="yom-event-year">1280</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Hyŏnhwa Monastery <span class="yom-hanja">玄化寺</span></h3><p>On the order of Ch’ungnyŏl and a royal princess, Yŏm Sŭngik has a new pavilion erected at the monastery. Here he acts as <strong>the executor of a royal commission</strong>.</p><p class="yom-source"><em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 29, 9a–b.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">royal mission</span><span class="yom-tag">architecture</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour commande monastere" id="scriptorium"><div class="yom-event-year">1281</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>A scriptorium in one of Yŏm Sŭngik’s dependencies</h3><p>He makes one of his dependencies available for the installation of the royal scriptorium devoted to copying the Great Canon in gold characters: <span class="yom-hanja">金字大藏寫經所</span>, <span class="yom-roman">Kŭmja taejang sagyŏngso</span>.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">scriptorium</span><span class="yom-tag">sūtras</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour monastere commande" id="timeline-1283"><div class="yom-event-year">1283</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Restoring the capital’s stupas</h3><p>Ch’ungnyŏl charges Yŏm Sŭngik and Kong Yu <span class="yom-hanja">孔愉</span> with supervising restorations at Hyŏnhwa, Wangnyun, Namgyewŏn, and a dependency of Kaeguk Monastery. Around the same time, Yŏm Sŭngik commissions the Lotus Sūtra associated with the Namgyewŏn stupa.</p><p class="yom-source"><em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 29, 45a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">royal mission</span><span class="yom-tag">personal patronage</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="commande rituel"><div class="yom-event-year">1286</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Amitābha <span class="yom-hanja">阿彌陀如來圖</span></h3><p>Yŏm Sŭngik commissions a painting of Amitābha to formulate vows for the royal family, his relatives, and rebirth in the Pure Land.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">painting</span><span class="yom-tag">vow</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour"><div class="yom-event-year">1289</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Journey to Dadu</h3><p>Yŏm Sŭngik accompanies the king and queen to Dadu, revealing his position within relations between Koryŏ and the Yuan.</p><p class="yom-source">See also Yŏm Sŭngik’s biography in the <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">court</span><span class="yom-tag">Yuan</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="commande rituel"><div class="yom-event-year">1292</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Dhāraṇī of the Precious Casket Seal <span class="yom-hanja">寶篋印陀羅尼</span></h3><p>A woodblock matrix and its impressions attest to another form of patronage: a reproducible textual image intended for ritual efficacy.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">woodblock printing</span><span class="yom-tag">dhāraṇī</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour"><div class="yom-event-year">1293</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Another journey to Dadu</h3><p>Yŏm Sŭngik again accompanies the royal couple.</p><p class="yom-source">See <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">court</span><span class="yom-tag">Yuan</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="cour rituel"><div class="yom-event-year">1295</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Withdrawal due to illness</h3><p>Illness leads Yŏm Sŭngik to withdraw from political affairs without ending his religious commitments.</p><p class="yom-source">See Yŏm Sŭngik’s biography in the <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">illness</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="rituel cour"><div class="yom-event-year">1297</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Ritual and healing</h3><p>During the illness of a royal princess, Yŏm Sŭngik is recalled to court and performs extreme devotional practices, showing the persistence of his reputation as a healer.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">ritual</span><span class="yom-tag">healing</span></div></div></article>
      <article class="yom-event" data-kind="rituel"><div class="yom-event-year">1302</div><div class="yom-event-body"><h3>Entering monastic life and death</h3><p>After refusing new appointments, Yŏm Sŭngik returns his titles, becomes a Buddhist monk, and dies in the same year.</p><p class="yom-source"><em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 32, 10a; see also k. 123, 8a–11a.</p><div class="yom-event-tags"><span class="yom-tag">monastic life</span></div></div></article>
    </div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="commanditaire"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">03 · An essential distinction</div><h2>Supervising for the king is not the same as commissioning for oneself</h2><p>The sources associate Yŏm Sŭngik with undertakings of different status. Conflating them would make him the commissioner of works that in fact originated with Ch’ungnyŏl.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-distinction">
      <article class="yom-distinction-card royal"><div class="yom-distinction-label">Royal mission · Ch’ungnyŏl gives the order</div><h3>Yŏm Sŭngik supervises or executes</h3><ul><li><strong>1280:</strong> erection of a pavilion at Hyŏnhwa Monastery <span class="yom-hanja">玄化寺</span>.</li><li><strong>1283:</strong> mission to restore stone stupas at several institutions in Kaegyŏng.</li></ul></article>
      <article class="yom-distinction-card personal"><div class="yom-distinction-label">Personal patronage · Yŏm Sŭngik formulates the vow</div><h3>Three surviving or documented works</h3><ul><li><strong>c. 1283:</strong> Lotus Sūtra <span class="yom-hanja">妙法蓮華經</span>.</li><li><strong>1286:</strong> painting of Amitābha <span class="yom-hanja">阿彌陀如來圖</span>.</li><li><strong>1292:</strong> Dhāraṇī of the Precious Casket Seal <span class="yom-hanja">寶篋印陀羅尼</span>.</li></ul></article>
    </div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="mission-1283"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">04 · Seventh lunar month of 1283</div><h2>The stupa-restoration mission</h2><p>After the destruction and damage connected with the Mongol wars, Ch’ungnyŏl entrusts Yŏm Sŭngik and Kong Yu with a mission among the Buddhist institutions of the capital. The itinerary documented in the dissertation links four sites.</p></div>
    <figure class="yom-map-insert">
      <img src="/assets/img/yom-sungik/map-tournee-1283.webp" alt="Map of Yŏm Sŭngik’s 1283 circuit to restore stupas in Kaegyŏng." loading="lazy">
      <figcaption><strong>Stupa-restoration circuit, 1283.</strong> The map visualises the mission entrusted to Yŏm Sŭngik and Kong Yu: Hyŏnhwasa, Wangnyunsa, Namgyewŏn, and a dependency of Kaeguksa. This was a royal mission supervised by Yŏm Sŭngik, not four personal commissions.</figcaption>
    </figure>
    <div class="yom-mission" aria-label="1283 restoration mission">
      <div class="yom-mission-step"><div class="num">01</div><h3>Hyŏnhwa</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">玄化寺</div><p>A monastery already linked to Yŏm Sŭngik through the royal architectural commission of 1280.</p></div>
      <div class="yom-mission-step"><div class="num">02</div><h3>Wangnyun</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">王輪寺</div><p>One of the capital’s major institutions included in the restoration program.</p></div>
      <div class="yom-mission-step"><div class="num">03</div><h3>Namgyewŏn</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">南溪院</div><p>The crucial case: the surviving stupa connects architecture, restoration, and the deposition of a sūtra.</p></div>
      <div class="yom-mission-step"><div class="num">04</div><h3>Kaeguk</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">開國寺</div><p>A dependency of the monastery also appears in the mission reported by the sources used in the dissertation.</p></div>
    </div>
    <p class="yom-source"><strong>Textual source:</strong> <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 29, 45a. The page does not artificially reconstruct the appearance of lost monuments: only Namgyewŏn is developed here as a material case study where the monument and associated objects are documented.</p>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="namgyewon"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">05 · Architecture and deposition</div><h2>Namgyewŏn <span class="yom-hanja">南溪院</span>: the stupa as a ritual container</h2><p>The seven-story stone stupa from the Namgyewŏn site near Kaesŏng is where Yŏm Sŭngik’s biography intersects most directly with the materiality of an object. When the monument was dismantled and relocated in the early twentieth century, Buddhist scrolls were discovered inside.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-media-grid">
      <figure class="yom-figure yom-image-reduced"><img src="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/Seven-story_Stone_Pagoda_from_Namgyewon_Temple_Site%2C_Gaeseong_%EB%82%A8%EA%B3%84%EC%9B%90%EC%A7%80_%EC%B9%A0%EC%B8%B5%EC%84%9D%ED%83%91.jpg" alt="Seven-story stone stupa from the Namgyewŏn site"><figcaption>Seven-story stone stupa from the Namgyewŏn site · <span class="yom-hanja">開城 南溪院址 七層石塔</span> · photograph Bart0278, CC BY-SA 3.0 · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Seven-story_Stone_Pagoda_from_Namgyewon_Temple_Site,_Gaeseong_%EB%82%A8%EA%B3%84%EC%9B%90%EC%A7%80_%EC%B9%A0%EC%B8%B5%EC%84%9D%ED%83%91.jpg" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Wikimedia Commons ↗</a></figcaption></figure>
      <div class="yom-text-panel"><div class="big-number">7</div><h3>stone stories, seven associated scrolls</h3><p>The monument is now preserved at the National Museum of Korea. The discovery of scrolls copied in metallic ink on indigo paper allows the stupa to be read not only as architecture, but also as a space of deposition.</p><dl>
        <dt>Name</dt><dd>Seven-story stone stupa from the Namgyewŏn site</dd><dt>Sinographs</dt><dd class="yom-hanja">南溪院址七層石塔</dd><dt>Provenance</dt><dd>Kaesŏng, kingdom of Koryŏ</dd><dt>Intervention</dt><dd>Restoration supervised by Yŏm Sŭngik in 1283 on royal order · <em>Koryŏsa</em>, k. 29, 45a</dd><dt>Status</dt><dd>National Treasure of Korea No. 100</dd>
      </dl></div>
    </div>
    <div class="yom-cutaway" aria-label="Diagram of the deposit inside the stupa">
      <div class="yom-pagoda" aria-hidden="true"><div class="yom-roof r1"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-roof r2"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-roof r3"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-roof r4"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-roof r5"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-roof r6"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-roof r7"></div><div class="yom-body"></div><div class="yom-base"><span class="yom-relic-slot" title="Ritual deposit"></span></div></div>
      <div class="yom-cutaway-flow">
        <div class="yom-flow-step"><div class="yom-flow-index">1</div><div><h3>Stone monument</h3><p>The stupa materializes Buddhist presence in the landscape of Kaegyŏng.</p></div></div>
        <div class="yom-flow-step"><div class="yom-flow-index">2</div><div><h3>Internal cavity</h3><p>Part of the architecture becomes inaccessible once sealed.</p></div></div>
        <div class="yom-flow-step"><div class="yom-flow-index">3</div><div><h3>Deposition of the sūtra</h3><p>The text is no longer intended for ordinary reading: it becomes a votive object incorporated into the monument.</p></div></div>
        <div class="yom-flow-step"><div class="yom-flow-index">4</div><div><h3>Reliquary presence</h3><p>In the interpretation developed in the dissertation, the sūtra functions as a relic and participates in the consecration of the stupa.</p></div></div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <figure class="yom-figure contain yom-image-reduced" style="max-width:980px;margin:42px auto 0;"><img src="https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/217c/11855048/9987ba0aac76/kjmh-33-3-563f5.jpg" alt="Historic photograph of the Namgyewŏn stupa and the seven scrolls found inside" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Historic photograph of the stupa and the seven scrolls discovered during its relocation · reproduced in Lim Young-ae, 2024 · <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11855048/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">open-access article ↗</a></figcaption></figure>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="lotus"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">06 · c. 1283</div><h2>The Lotus Sūtra <span class="yom-hanja">妙法蓮華經</span>: a “sūtra as relic”</h2><p>The colophon identifies Yŏm Sŭngik as the commissioner. Its association with the restoration of the Namgyewŏn stupa gives the work a function beyond luxury copying: it was conceived for deposition within a consecration device.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-media-grid">
      <figure class="yom-figure contain yom-image-reduced"><img src="https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/217c/11855048/9997c4b7344a/kjmh-33-3-563f4.jpg" alt="Votive text of the Lotus Sūtra commissioned by Yŏm Sŭngik" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Votive text associated with Yŏm Sŭngik’s Lotus Sūtra · reproduced in Lim Young-ae, 2024 · <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11855048/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">source ↗</a></figcaption></figure>
      <div class="yom-text-panel"><div class="big-number">1283</div><h3>Text, image, and deposition</h3><dl><dt>Title</dt><dd>Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma</dd><dt>Sinographs</dt><dd class="yom-hanja">妙法蓮華經</dd><dt>Romanization</dt><dd><span class="yom-roman">Myobŏp yŏnhwagyŏng</span></dd><dt>Commissioner</dt><dd>Yŏm Sŭngik <span class="yom-hanja">廉承益</span></dd><dt>Support</dt><dd>Indigo paper, metallic-ink writing</dd><dt>Function</dt><dd>Vow, consecration, and deposition inside the stupa</dd></dl></div>
    </div>
    <div class="yom-lotus-analysis" aria-labelledby="lotus-image-analysis-title">
      <figure class="yom-lotus-frontispiece">
        <img src="/assets/img/yom-sungik/namgyewon-lotus-frontispiece.webp" alt="Frontispiece of the first roll of the Namgyewŏn Lotus Sūtra, showing a wrathful protective figure painted in gold on indigo paper" loading="lazy">
        <figcaption>Frontispiece of the first roll of the <em>Lotus Sūtra</em> <span class="yom-hanja">妙法蓮華經</span> from Namgyewŏn, c. 1283 · indigo paper, gold and silver · National Museum of Korea.</figcaption>
      </figure>
      <div class="yom-lotus-analysis-copy">
        <div class="yom-kicker">Image analysis</div>
        <h3 id="lotus-image-analysis-title">A protective figure condensed within a “sūtra as relic”</h3>
        <p>The first of the seven rolls discovered in the stupa <span class="yom-hanja">塔</span> at Namgyewŏn is the best preserved. On indigo-dyed paper, the text is copied in silver, while the cover and frontispiece are executed in gold. The image is remarkable for its iconographic economy: rather than presenting an extended narrative scene, it isolates a single wrathful figure standing on a lotus throne <span class="yom-hanja">蓮華座</span> and holding a large vajra <span class="yom-hanja">金剛杵</span> (<span class="yom-roman">kŭmgangjŏ</span>) in the right hand.</p>
        <p>The body turns to the left while the head twists in the opposite direction. The pronounced musculature, animated folds of the garment, tension of the arms, and flames surrounding the head give the figure an energetic, protective presence. The composition does not seek to narrate the contents of the sūtra; instead, it concentrates the power of the Dharma <span class="yom-hanja">法</span> into an immediately legible image. Stylistically, it is very close to protective figures in illustrated sūtras <span class="yom-hanja">經</span> produced around 1275–1276, notably the <em>Sūtra of the Mantras of the Miraculous Transformations of the Amoghapāśa</em> and the <em>Sūtra of the Bodhisattva <span class="yom-hanja">菩薩</span> Mañjuśrī <span class="yom-hanja">文殊師利</span></em>.</p>
        <p>This simplicity becomes especially meaningful when the manuscript’s destination is considered. The seven rolls were not intended to remain visible: they were deposited inside the stupa <span class="yom-hanja">塔</span> restored in 1283. The image should therefore be understood less as an aid to contemplation than as a <strong>condensed and operative ritual presence</strong>. Such an object can be understood as a <strong>“sūtra as relic”</strong>: the sacred text, its protective image, and the monument enclosing them together form a device of consecration. This interpretation resonates with the passage in the <em>Lotus Sūtra</em> <span class="yom-hanja">妙法蓮華經</span> that equates the presence of the text with that of the very body of the Tathāgata <span class="yom-hanja">如來</span>.</p>
        <p class="yom-source">The manuscript commissioned by Yŏm Sŭngik around 1283 and discovered in the Namgyewŏn stupa is preserved in the National Museum of Korea.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="yom-inscription"><div class="yom-kicker">A shared votive motif</div><div class="hanja yom-hanja" lang="zh-Hant">願我臨欲命終時 · 盡除一切諸障礙 · 面見彼佛阿彌陀 · 即得往生安樂刹</div><div class="translation">“When the moment of my death comes, may all obstacles be dispelled; may I behold the Buddha Amitābha face to face and immediately be reborn in the Land of Peace.”</div><div class="note">This gāthā connects the Lotus Sūtra commissioned by Yŏm Sŭngik with the Amitābha painting of 1286. The translation is provided here to make the sense of the vow legible; the full colophon is more extensive.</div></div>
    <div class="yom-practice-flow" aria-label="Function of the sūtra as relic"><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Copy</b><small>materially produce the sacred text</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Formulate the vow</b><small>king, relatives, commissioner</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Deposit</b><small>place the scrolls inside the stupa</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Seal</b><small>remove the object from view</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Consecrate</b><small>make the text an operative presence</small></div></div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="amitabha"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">07 · 1286</div><h2>Amitābha <span class="yom-hanja">阿彌陀如來圖</span>: prayer becomes image</h2><p>Three years after the restoration of Namgyewŏn, Yŏm Sŭngik commissions a painting of Amitābha. Its inscription prays for the happiness and longevity of the king, the princess, and Yŏm Sŭngik’s relatives, while reaffirming the hope of rebirth in the Pure Land.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-media-grid">
      <figure class="yom-figure contain yom-image-reduced"><img src="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/Amitabha_%28former_Shimazu_collection%29.jpg" alt="Painting of Amitābha commissioned by Yŏm Sŭngik in 1286" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Amitābha, 1286, former Shimazu collection · public domain · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Amitabha_(former_Shimazu_collection).jpg" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Wikimedia Commons ↗</a></figcaption></figure>
      <div class="yom-text-panel"><div class="big-number">1286</div><h3>From writing to devotional image</h3><dl><dt>Title</dt><dd>Painting of the Buddha Amitābha</dd><dt>Sinographs</dt><dd class="yom-hanja">阿彌陀如來圖</dd><dt>Romanization</dt><dd><span class="yom-roman">Amit’a yŏraedo</span></dd><dt>Commissioner</dt><dd>Yŏm Sŭngik <span class="yom-hanja">廉承益</span></dd><dt>Date</dt><dd>1286 · Zhiyuan 23 <span class="yom-hanja">至元二十三年</span></dd><dt>Vow</dt><dd>Longevity, protection, and rebirth in Amitābha’s Pure Land</dd></dl><p style="margin-top:24px;">The connection with the Lotus Sūtra is not merely chronological: the same four-line gāthā appears in both ensembles. The writing deposited within the stupa and the image made for devotion therefore participate in the same votive horizon.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="dharani"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">08 · 1292</div><h2>The dhāraṇī becomes matrix and image</h2><p>The Dhāraṇī of the Precious Casket Seal <span class="yom-hanja">寶篋印陀羅尼</span>, produced under Yŏm Sŭngik’s supervision, introduces a different material logic: no longer a unique object, but a matrix enabling the multiplication of impressions intended for ritual use.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-media-grid">
      <figure class="yom-figure contain yom-image-reduced"><img src="https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/217c/11855048/8ae5e7ed0cc9/kjmh-33-3-563f7.jpg" alt="Precious Casket Seal Dhāraṇī-maṇḍala associated with Yŏm Sŭngik, 1292" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Precious Casket Seal Dhāraṇī-maṇḍala, 1292 · reproduced in Lim Young-ae, 2024 · <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11855048/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">source ↗</a></figcaption></figure>
      <div class="yom-text-panel"><div class="big-number">1292</div><h3>A reproducible textual image</h3><p>The object combines text, diagrammatic structure, and ritual power. Woodblock printing transforms the nature of Yŏm Sŭngik’s patronage: a single matrix can generate multiple impressions that then circulate in contexts of consecration.</p><dl><dt>Technique</dt><dd>Woodblock printing</dd><dt>Text</dt><dd>Dhāraṇī of the Precious Casket Seal <span class="yom-hanja">寶篋印陀羅尼</span></dd><dt>Yŏm Sŭngik’s role</dt><dd>Supervision attested by the inscription associated with production</dd><dt>Function</dt><dd>Protection, merit, and ritual efficacy</dd></dl></div>
    </div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="trois-oeuvres"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">09 · Three milestones</div><h2>1283 → 1286 → 1292: tracing Yŏm Sŭngik’s personal patronage</h2><p>Rather than isolating each work by medium, their sequence shows how the same concerns—protection, longevity, merit, and salvation—move from manuscript writing to painting and then to the printed image.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-objects">
      <article class="yom-object"><img src="https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/217c/11855048/9987ba0aac76/kjmh-33-3-563f5.jpg" alt="Scrolls associated with the Namgyewŏn stupa" loading="lazy"><div class="yom-object-body"><div class="yom-object-year">c. 1283 · WRITING</div><h3>Lotus Sūtra</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">妙法蓮華經</div><p>Votive copying, deposition in the stupa, and transformation of the text into a reliquary presence.</p></div></article>
      <article class="yom-object tall"><img src="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/Amitabha_%28former_Shimazu_collection%29.jpg" alt="Amitābha commissioned by Yŏm Sŭngik in 1286" loading="lazy"><div class="yom-object-body"><div class="yom-object-year">1286 · IMAGE</div><h3>Amitābha</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">阿彌陀如來圖</div><p>A devotional painting that reiterates the same votive horizon of rebirth in the Pure Land.</p></div></article>
      <article class="yom-object"><img src="https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/217c/11855048/8ae5e7ed0cc9/kjmh-33-3-563f7.jpg" alt="Dhāraṇī-maṇḍala associated with Yŏm Sŭngik, 1292" loading="lazy"><div class="yom-object-body"><div class="yom-object-year">1292 · PRINT</div><h3>Dhāraṇī</h3><div class="hanja yom-hanja">寶篋印陀羅尼</div><p>The woodblock matrix enables the multiplication of ritual objects without separating text from image.</p></div></article>
    </div>
    <div class="yom-practice-flow" aria-label="Evolution of Yŏm Sŭngik’s personal patronage"><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Commissioner</b><small>Yŏm Sŭngik 廉承益</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Intention</b><small>protect · prolong life</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Practice</b><small>copy · image · print</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Object</b><small>sūtra · painting · dhāraṇī</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Horizon</b><small>merit · salvation · Pure Land</small></div></div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="kaegyong"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">10 · Kaegyŏng 開京</div><h2>A trajectory embedded in the capital’s Buddhist institutions</h2><p>Yŏm Sŭngik’s trajectory intersects with several major monasteries of Kaegyŏng, but this page does not duplicate the general map of the capital’s Buddhist networks. It isolates only Yŏm Sŭngik’s own path: <strong>Ch’ŏnhyo → Hyŏnhwa → royal scriptorium → stupa mission → Namgyewŏn</strong>.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-practice-flow" aria-label="Yŏm Sŭngik’s path through Kaegyŏng’s Buddhist institutions"><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Ch’ŏnhyo</b><small><span class="yom-hanja">天孝寺</span> · 1277</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Hyŏnhwa</b><small><span class="yom-hanja">玄化寺</span> · 1280</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Scriptorium</b><small><span class="yom-hanja">金字大藏寫經所</span> · 1281</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Royal mission</b><small>several stupas · 1283</small></div><div class="yom-practice-step"><b>Namgyewŏn</b><small><span class="yom-hanja">南溪院</span> · sūtra deposit</small></div></div>
  <figure class="yom-map-insert">
      <img src="/assets/img/yom-sungik/map-kaegyong-dadu.webp" alt="Map of Yŏm Sŭngik’s routes between Kaegyŏng and Dadu, including the court journeys of 1289 and 1293." loading="lazy">
      <figcaption><strong>From Kaegyŏng to Dadu.</strong> The journeys of 1289 and 1293 place Yŏm Sŭngik within a broader political space: his activities in Kaegyŏng’s Buddhist institutions intersect with his role as an intermediary between the Koryŏ court and the Yuan world.</figcaption>
    </figure>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="dernieres-annees"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">11 · 1295–1302</div><h2>Illness, withdrawal, and entry into monastic life</h2><p>The final phase of Yŏm Sŭngik’s life gives further coherence to his religious patronage. In 1295, ill health leads him to withdraw from political affairs. Two years later, his reputation as a healer brings him back into contact with the royal family. In 1302, after refusing new appointments, he relinquishes his titles and becomes a Buddhist monk shortly before his death.</p><p class="yom-source">For the biographical trajectory: <em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a; for 1302: k. 32, 10a.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-legacy"><article class="yom-legacy-card"><div class="mark">1295</div><h3>Withdrawal</h3><p>Illness interrupts his active political career, but not his religious practices.</p></article><article class="yom-legacy-card"><div class="mark">1297</div><h3>Healing and devotion</h3><p>The court continues to call on Yŏm Sŭngik in therapeutic and ritual contexts.</p></article><article class="yom-legacy-card"><div class="mark">1302</div><h3>Buddhist monk</h3><p>His final renunciation of court titles closes a trajectory in which political office and Buddhist commitment had constantly coexisted.</p></article></div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section" id="conclusion"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">12 · What the case of Yŏm Sŭngik reveals</div><h2>An intermediary rather than merely a commissioner</h2><p>Yŏm Sŭngik allows us to understand Buddhist art in Koryŏ as the product of coordinated actions: a royal decision, an administrative mission, a monastery, a scriptorium, a votive object, and a ritual gesture could all belong to the same chain of action.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-legacy"><article class="yom-legacy-card"><div class="mark yom-hanja">王</div><h3>The man of power</h3><p>His proximity to Ch’ungnyŏl gives him access to court resources and major Buddhist institutions.</p></article><article class="yom-legacy-card"><div class="mark yom-hanja">願</div><h3>The practitioner</h3><p>Colophons and inscriptions reveal personal concerns: health, protection, merit, and rebirth in the Pure Land.</p></article><article class="yom-legacy-card"><div class="mark yom-hanja">像</div><h3>The intermediary</h3><p>He connects architecture, manuscript, painting, and printing without these media sharing the same function or commissioning status.</p></article></div>
  </div></section>

  <section class="yom-section yom-sources" id="sources"><div class="yom-shell">
    <div class="yom-section-head"><div class="yom-kicker">Sources & method</div><h2>A page built from the dissertation</h2><p>The text and interpretive structure are based first on the dissertation chapters devoted to Yŏm Sŭngik, the Lotus Sūtra from Namgyewŏn, and Buddhist production under Ch’ungnyŏl. Factual elements have been cross-checked against primary sources and recent scholarship.</p></div>
    <div class="yom-sources-grid">
      <div><h3>Main sources</h3><ul>
        <li><em>Koryŏsa</em> <span class="yom-hanja">高麗史</span>, k. 123, 8a–11a: biography of Yŏm Sŭngik in the section on “favorites”.</li>
        <li><em>Koryŏsa</em>, k. 123, 10a–b: Yŏm Sŭngik’s reputation, proximity to the court, and Buddhist activities.</li>
        <li><em>Koryŏsa</em>, k. 29, 9a–b: royal order concerning the pavilion at Hyŏnhwa Monastery in 1280.</li>
        <li><em>Koryŏsa</em>, k. 29, 45a: the 1283 mission to restore the stupas of Hyŏnhwa, Wangnyun, Namgyewŏn, and a dependency of Kaeguk.</li>
        <li><em>Koryŏsa</em>, k. 32, 10a: Yŏm Sŭngik’s final years and entry into monastic life in 1302.</li>
        <li>Bryan Sauvadet’s dissertation, chapters 1 and 2, sections devoted to Yŏm Sŭngik and Koryŏ sūtras.</li>
        <li><a href="https://www.museum.go.kr/ENG/contents/E0201070000.do?schM=view&id=100252" target="_blank" rel="noopener">National Museum of Korea — Namgyewŏn stupa ↗</a></li>
        <li><a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11855048/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Lim Young-ae, study of Yŏm Sŭngik, illness, healing, and Buddhist practice ↗</a></li>
        <li><a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/rel17070769" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Lim Young-ae, study of works commissioned by Yŏm Sŭngik ↗</a></li>
      </ul></div>
      <div><h3>Editorial principles</h3><ul><li>Korean romanization follows the <strong>McCune–Reischauer</strong> system.</li><li>Sinographs are supplied at the first occurrence of major persons, institutions, and works.</li><li>An explicit distinction is maintained between <strong>royal mission</strong> and <strong>personal patronage</strong>.</li><li>Cautious dating (“c. 1283”) is used when an exact year is not secured by the object itself.</li><li>Graphic reconstructions are explanatory infographics, not archaeological restitutions.</li></ul></div>
    </div>
